title: Native American Reservations
summary: Hosts give a broad overview of Native American reservations in the United States: how the reservation system evolved from forced removal and treaties through the Indian Appropriations Act of 1851, the Dawes Act, the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, the termination era, and the Indian Self-Determination and Education Act of 1975. They explain the trust-land status and tribal sovereignty, the patchwork of tribal courts, law enforcement and schools, Alaska's shared reservation and dividend system, and language and culture revitalization. They compare the Navajo Nation (largest, unusually returned to ancestral lands), Pine Ridge in South Dakota (severe poverty, low life expectancy, White Clay beer sales), and the Seminole Tribe of Florida (casino wealth, Hard Rock brand). They also discuss federal administrations' Native policy, voter registration efforts, and close with a listener email about diaries.
topics: Indian Self-Determination and Education Act of 1975

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, a recommendation of the TV show Reservation Dogs and the film Smoke Signals, and frame the episode as a broad overview. They discuss land taken from Native peoples through both treaties and seizure, and the lasting effects of the reservation system.

segments.title: Population and reservation sovereignty
segments.summary: Census figures show about 9.7 million people identified as Alaska Native or American Indian in 2020, with about 1.2 million (13 percent) living on reservations. Reservations are described as sovereign nations with their own rules, which explains casinos and cheap cigarettes and limits state jurisdiction.

segments.title: McGirt v. Oklahoma
segments.summary: Oklahoma, about half reservation land, tried to prosecute tribal members for crimes on tribal land. A 2020 Supreme Court ruling in McGirt v. Oklahoma held states lack jurisdiction, leading to dismissed cases.

segments.title: History: removal, treaties, and allotment
segments.summary: Hosts trace the history from forced westward removal and broken treaties, to the Indian Appropriations Act of 1851 creating a federal reservation system, the 1850s to 1880s period of food dependence, the Dawes Act of 1887 breaking reservations into family plots, the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 allowing land repurchase, the termination era, and the 1975 Indian Self-Determination and Education Act.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break before returning to the modern system.

segments.title: Shifting federal policies and their toll
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on repeated policy shifts by successive administrations and the whiplash of removal and reservation policy over less than a century, and on why the public tends to forget this history.

segments.title: Modern land trust and reservation types
segments.summary: There are 325 tracts of land held in trust by the US government, with varied names such as reservations, villages, missions, pueblos, and rancherias. The Navajo Nation is the largest and the Likely Rancheria in California is among the smallest. Trust status keeps land out of state taxation and jurisdiction.

segments.title: Non-native residents, Oneida, California rancherias, and patchwork systems
segments.summary: Non-Native people can live on reservations, and the Oneida Indian Nation in upstate New York has about 500 American Indian residents among about 60,000 total. The Oneida's Turning Stone Resort and casino is a major employer. California rancherias were created in the twentieth century. Reservation arrangements vary and developed locally.

segments.title: Alaska's shared reservation and dividends
segments.summary: Alaska has 279 federally recognized tribes, more than half of the federally recognized tribes, sharing one reservation. Resource extraction revenue funds dividends to enrolled Alaska Natives. Hawaii has a similar system but no reservations.

segments.title: Sovereignty and Marshall's domestic dependent nations
segments.summary: Tribes are recognized as sovereign nations under the Constitution. Chief Justice John Marshall's 1831 ruling called tribes domestic dependent nations, a status the hosts say is confusing and open to interpretation.

segments.title: Tribal courts, police, and schools
segments.summary: Some tribes have their own courts, while others are served by five Courts of Indian Offenses. Tribes often run their own law enforcement, sometimes alongside Bureau of Indian Affairs police, and Alaska has a Village Public Safety Officer program. Reservations have their own school districts and boarding schools.

segments.title: Boarding schools and language revitalization
segments.summary: Hosts describe abusive boarding schools and the current push to restore Native culture and languages. The Cherokee Nation has about 2,000 fluent speakers left, losing about 150 a year, and runs the Durbin Feeling Language Center. In 2022 the US government gave seven million dollars in grants to 45 tribes for language preservation.

segments.title: Federal administrations and Native policy
segments.summary: Hosts compare the Obama, Trump, and Biden administrations on Native issues. Biden-era items include seven million for languages, twenty-one million for road safety, and 135 million for climate-related relocation; Deb Haaland is noted as the first Native American Interior Secretary. Trump-era criticisms include the Council on Native American Affairs not being re-established and the Winnemucca reservation being disestablished.
topics: Obama Council on Native American Affairs

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before the reservation case studies.

segments.title: Navajo Nation
segments.summary: The Navajo Nation spans Utah, Arizona, and New Mexico, with about 400,000 enrolled members and 170,000 on the reservation. Unusually, the Navajo negotiated a treaty to return to ancestral lands within four years of removal. Its government has twenty-four districts, a council, and eleven court districts. Thirty-six percent of households are below poverty level and about the same share lack running water. Internet access is patchy.

segments.title: Pine Ridge Reservation and Oglala Sioux
segments.summary: Pine Ridge, about 4,000 square miles in South Dakota, is the largest Lakota reservation. It is tied to the Wounded Knee massacre of 1890, the 1970s AIM protests, and Standing Rock in 2015. It has very high unemployment, an infant mortality rate about five times the national average, and a life expectancy of 48 for men and 52 for women. White Clay, Nebraska sells beer to Lakota residents of the dry reservation.

segments.title: Seminole Tribe of Florida and Hard Rock
segments.summary: The Seminole Tribe of Florida, descended from people who hid in the Florida swamps, adopted a constitution in the 1950s and is thriving through casinos. The tribe owns the Hard Rock brand, bought in 2006, and its per-member payouts are large. The first Hard Rock was in Jackson, Tennessee, per the hosts' anecdote. The Seminole casino was the first Native casino, and its state lawsuit helped spark the spread of casinos.

segments.title: Native voter registration
segments.summary: Native Americans on reservations can vote in federal elections, but only about 60 percent of eligible Native Americans are registered. The Million Vote Opportunity campaign aims to register over a million eligible voters.

segments.title: Listener mail: Dear Diary and Martha Ballard
segments.summary: A listener named Casey recommends the diary history of Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, author of A Midwife's Tale about Martha Ballard's diary in Augusta, Maine from 1785 to 1812. The hosts thank Casey and ask for emails.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits for iHeartRadio.
